paras: The beating of James Gale was a mob assault on the night of 24 June 1903, in which a crowd knocked down and severely beat Gale, a Black man of 716 Wilson Street, at Fifth and King streets, apparently in Wilmington, Delaware. Gale escaped to the police station, where his injuries were dressed. He was one of a number of Black people attacked in the streets that night, and the only one named in the reports.

The attack took place during a night of disorder that followed the burning of a Black man named White by a mob and the arrest of Arthur Corwell, the only man held in the killing. According to the New-York Tribune, Corwell was released on bail that evening and handed over to a cheering crowd outside City Hall, and afterward the streets stayed full of men "in an ugly mood" until late. The same dispatch described Black men dragged from street cars and chased and beaten while the police were unable to stop the crowd.

The Evening Journal reported that Gale was "passing quietly along" when the crowd saw him at Fifth and King streets. He was knocked down and beaten, got back on his feet, and ran to the police station, where his injuries were dressed. A Wilmington wire printed in the Indianapolis Journal told of an unnamed Black man beaten "by a gang of whites" near the police station who took refuge inside, which may describe the same attack.

Other attacks took place that night: a Black band near Eighth and Market streets fled when young men and boys rushed toward it, and about seventy-five men threw bricks at houses occupied by Black residents on Orange Street.
No report of an arrest or charge in Gale's beating appears in the coverage.

Only the Evening Journal named Gale, in a short item headed "Lawlessness of Boys" with the subhead "Crowds of Them Attack Defenseless Colored People," which blamed "crowds of young men and boys" for the night's "outrages" on Black people. Out-of-town papers folded the street beatings into larger stories about the lynching and Corwell's release: the New-York Tribune's headline spoke of "Negroes Dragged from Cars in Wilmington and Chased and Beaten in the Streets," and the Indianapolis Journal's wire set the beating near the police station beside a street fight it said a Black man had started.

Four days later a commentary in the New York Sun blamed a "negro-baiting mob" for beating Black passengers on Wednesday night and said these attacks had awakened "the spirit of retaliation" among Black residents; no Black-press account of Gale's beating was found.
